studies.title: 2025-03 Sample Portal Appointment Reminders Usability Testing
studies.summary: A moderated usability study of a redesigned reminder settings page. Most participants wanted text messages first, did not trust reminders that omitted the clinic name, and rarely found the settings page without help.
keyFindings: Most participants wanted reminders by text message first, then email.
Participants did not trust a reminder that did not name the clinic.
Only two of eight participants found the reminder settings without help.

studies.title: 2025-06 Sample Portal Notification Preferences Discovery
studies.summary: Discovery interviews about how people choose notification settings. Participants set preferences once and forget them, treat changes to a date or a payment as essential, and switch everything off when alerts pile up.
keyFindings: Participants treated notification settings as set once and forget.
Essential meant anything that changes a date or a payment.
Too many alerts led participants to switch everything off.

studies.title: 2025-09 Sample Mobile App Sign-in Help Interviews
studies.summary: Remote interviews about choosing a sign-in option on the mobile app. Participants hesitated at the list of options and read help text only after a failed attempt.
keyFindings: Participants were unsure which sign-in option to choose.
Help text was read only after a failed attempt.

studies.title: 2026-01 Sample Portal Document Upload Usability Testing
studies.summary: A usability study of a new upload confirmation step. Participants wanted an immediate confirmation that repeated the file name, and a progress bar with no result left them unsure the upload finished.
keyFindings: Participants expected an immediate confirmation with the file name.
A progress bar without a result made participants unsure the upload finished.
Confirmation emails were wanted, but not for every upload.

lines: # Appointment Reminders Research Plan
## Background
Sample Portal sends appointment reminders, but people can only change them from a page that is hard to find. This study tests a redesigned reminder settings page.
## Research Goals
- Learn whether participants can find and change their reminder settings.
- Learn what a reminder needs to say for participants to trust it.
## Research Questions
- How do participants decide whether to turn appointment reminders on or off?
- What do participants expect a reminder to say, and when do they expect to receive it?
- Where do participants look first to change how they are reminded?
## Methodology
Moderated remote usability sessions, 45 minutes each, with a clickable prototype.
## Recruitment
Eight participants. Mix of desktop and phone users; at least two who use a screen reader.

lines: # Conversation Guide
## Moderator logistics
Share the prototype link in chat. Ask for consent to record before starting.
## Intro - 5 minutes
Explain that we are testing the page, not the participant. There are no wrong answers.
## Warm-up Questions - 5 minutes
- Tell me about the last time you missed or nearly missed an appointment.
- How do you usually keep track of your appointments?
## First Task: Find reminder settings - 20 minutes
- Where would you go to change how you are reminded about an appointment?
- What do you expect to see on this page?
- How would you turn off reminders for one appointment only?
## Thank-you and Closing - 5 minutes
- Is there anything you expected to see that was not there?

lines: # Appointment Reminders Research Findings
## Research Goals
- Learn whether participants can find and change their reminder settings.
## Research Questions
- How do participants decide whether to turn appointment reminders on or off?
- Where do participants look first to change how they are reminded?
## Methodology
Eight moderated remote sessions in March 2025. Two participants used a screen reader.
## Key Findings
### Most participants wanted reminders by text message first, then email
Six of eight participants asked for text messages. Email was seen as something to check later.
> _“I just want a text the day before. If I have to log in to find out, it is too late.” - P2_
> _“Email is fine as a backup, but I do not look at it until the evening.” - P5_
### Participants did not trust a reminder that did not name the clinic
A reminder that only said “you have an appointment” led four participants to ask whether it was real.
> _“If it does not say where, I would think it is a scam.” - P4_
> _“I would want the clinic name and the time, nothing else.”_
### Few participants found the reminder settings without help
Only two participants found the settings page on their own. Most looked under their profile first.
> _“I looked under my name. It never occurred to me to look at the appointment itself.” - P7_

lines: # Notification Preferences Discovery Plan
## Background
People receive notifications from several parts of Sample Portal. We do not know which ones they consider essential.
## Research Questions
- How do people decide whether to turn notifications on or off?
- Which notification types do people consider essential?
- What makes someone stop trusting a notification?
## Methodology
Eight 60-minute remote interviews.

lines: # Notification Preferences Discovery Findings
## Research Questions
- How do people decide whether to turn notifications on or off?
- Which notification types do people consider essential?
## Key Findings
### Participants treated notification settings as set once and forget
Most participants could not remember what they had chosen and had not looked at the settings since.
> _“I turned something on once. I could not tell you what.” - P1_
### Essential meant anything that changes a date or a payment
Participants agreed that changes to a date, a time or an amount owed were essential, and the rest could wait.
> _“Tell me if something moves or if I owe something. The rest is noise.” - P3_
> _“A new message is not urgent. A cancelled appointment is.” - P6_
### Too many alerts led participants to switch everything off
> _“After the third one in a day I turned them all off.” - P8_

lines: # Mobile Sign-in Help Research Findings
## Research Questions
- Which sign-in option do participants choose, and why?
- What do participants do when sign-in fails?
## Key Findings
### Participants were unsure which sign-in option to choose
Five of seven participants hesitated at the list of options and chose the one they had used on the website.
> _“I picked the one I remembered from the website. I did not read the others.” - P2_
> _“There were too many buttons and none of them said which one was mine.” - Caregiver_
### Help text was read only after a failed attempt
No participant opened the help text before trying to sign in. Three opened it after a first failure.
> _“I only looked at the help when it said it did not work.” - P5_

lines: # Document Upload Research Plan
## Background
People upload documents to support a request, then call to ask whether the upload worked. We are testing a new confirmation step.
## Research Questions
- What do participants expect to happen after they upload a document?
- How do participants know an upload worked?
- How do participants decide whether to turn confirmation emails on or off?
## Methodology
Ten moderated remote usability sessions.

lines: # Document Upload Research Findings
## Research Questions
- What do participants expect to happen after they upload a file?
- How do participants know an upload worked?
## Key Findings
### Participants expected an immediate confirmation with the file name
Nine of ten participants said a confirmation that repeated the file name would be enough to trust the upload.
> _“Show me the name of what I sent. Then I know it is the right one.” - P1_
### A progress bar without a result made participants unsure the upload finished
> _“It filled up and then it just went away. Did it work?” - P4_
> _“I would have taken a screenshot, honestly.” - P9_
### Confirmation emails were wanted, but not for every upload
Participants wanted an email for the first upload and a quieter option after that.

lines: # Caregiver Account Linking Discovery Plan
## Background
Caregivers manage appointments and documents for someone else. Today they share a login, which we want to stop.
## Research Questions
- How do caregivers expect to be connected to the person they support?
- What information would caregivers be comfortable sharing to link accounts?
- How do caregivers decide whether to turn notifications on or off for the person they support?
## Methodology
Twelve 60-minute remote interviews with caregivers.

limits: SAMPLE DATA: every study, participant and quote in this file is fictional. It exists so the app runs without access to a real research repository.
Questions and quotes are extracted from single lines only; quotes split across lines are not captured.
Session timestamps are captured only when written beside a quote in the source; most sources do not record them.
Board studies without a local folder have summary and key findings only, not the questions asked.
